stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Pick a nuclear reaction and study the ledger — a tiny amount of mass ($\Delta m$) disappears and re-appears as energy $E$. Try all $3$ reactions and drag the $\Delta m$ slider to see how $E$ scales. Advance when you've explored all three reactions.
stages.concept: Einstein's equivalence: $E = \Delta m \, c^2$, with $c = 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$. In a nuclear reaction the total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the reactants — the missing mass $\Delta m$ is released as energy. Working in atomic units, the useful shortcut is $1\,\text{u} \cdot c^2 = 931.5\,\text{MeV}$, so $E\,(\text{MeV}) = \Delta m\,(\text{u}) \times 931.5$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Given a mass defect $\Delta m$ in atomic units, compute the released energy $E$ in MeV. The unit-converter card at the bottom shows the constant you need. Type your answer and press ✓ (or Enter).
stages.concept: Direct application: $E\,(\text{MeV}) = \Delta m\,(\text{u}) \times 931.5$. Multiply — no square-roots, no logs. Tolerance is $\pm 3\%$ (or $\pm 0.5\,\text{MeV}$, whichever is larger).

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The unit-converter helper is hidden. Compute $E$ in MeV from $\Delta m$ in u using the constant from memory. Peek briefly re-reveals the helper if you're stuck.
stages.concept: Memorize the shortcut: $1\,\text{u} \to 931.5\,\text{MeV}$. Whenever a mass defect is given in $\text{u}$ and you want energy in MeV, multiply by $\approx 931.5$. This is one of the most-used constants in nuclear physics — worth memorizing exactly.

1.1: Click each reaction chip on the right. Notice how the ledger sums the masses on each side.
1.2: The missing mass Δm (before − after) becomes energy via E = Δm · c².
1.3: Try all 3 reactions AND drag the Δm slider at least once. That completes stage 1.

2.1: Use the constant on the helper card: E (MeV) = Δm (u) × 931.5.
2.3: Round to 1 decimal place; the tolerance is ±3% (or ±0.5 MeV).

3.1: Same formula as stage 2: E (MeV) = Δm (u) × 931.5. The helper is just hidden.
3.2: For Δm = 0.020 u, E ≈ 18.63 MeV. Peek reveals the helper briefly if you forgot.
3.3: Memorize this: 1 u ↔ 931.5 MeV. It's the most-used conversion in nuclear energy problems.
